en: Advayavajra’s *Tattvaratnāvalī*. Homage to Śrī Vajrasattva! Having bowed before the two lotus-feet of Vajrasattva, whose splendor is as stainless as the autumn moon, we shall speak this *Tattvaratnāvalī*.
(1) For those whose vision is shrouded by darkness due to having fallen away from the traditional lineage of the true teachings,
this *Tattvaratnāvalī* shall properly illuminate the reality for such persons.
(2) (The Introduction) In this regard, there are three vehicles: the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.
There are four systems of tenets,
distinguished as Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika.
Among these, the Śrāvakayāna and Pratyekabuddhayāna are explained according to the Vaibhāṣika system.
The Mahāyāna is twofold: the Pāramitānaya and the Mantranaya.
Among these, the Pāramitānaya is explained according to the systems of the Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika.
The Mantra system, however, is explained according to the position of the Yogācāra-Mādhyamika;
and the Yogācāra is of two kinds,
distinguished as Sākāra (with aspects) and Nirākāra (without aspects).
In this way, the Mādhyamika is also twofold due to the distinction between those who assert that all phenomena are like an illusion and those who assert that they are non-abiding.
Among these, the Śrāvaka [vehicle] is threefold.
This is due to the distinction between weak, medium, and intense.
In this context, the weak and medium [positions] belong to the Western Vaibhāṣikas,
while the intense belongs to the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas.
I. Regarding that, the investigation of the inferior śrāvaka is as follows:
the commentary states that he first accepts external objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth, and then teaches the dissociation of the person from being either eternal or impermanent.
As it has been said: "(p1) 'The world, consisting of blue and so forth, truly exists'—this is for the sake of those who are dull-witted."
To the one who is terrified by the profound method [of emptiness], which is like the onset of a seizure from the demon of grasping at existence.
(3) There is a person who says: "I do not say that the bearer of the burden is permanent, nor do I say that he is impermanent.
And since the person, possessed of passion, wanders in saṃsāra, meditation on the foul is for the sake of abandoning passion.
Meditation on the foul, however, is the discernment of the body as being a composite of excrement, urine, semen, blood, phlegm, intestines, entrails, lungs, spleen, liver, and so forth.
Thus it has been said: "First, separate this skin-sack from your own mind;
then, with the sword of wisdom, strip the flesh away from the skeleton."
(4) Even having separated the bones, look at the marrow within;
investigate for yourself whether there is any essence here.
(5) Thus:
the prior ascent based on the view of the permanence of the person (*pudgala*) is a defilement of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

Furthermore, what is the view that [the two] Sugatas or Buddhas are to be worshipped, while thinking: "I shall subdue this one self, I shall pacify this one self, I shall cause this one self to attain final nirvana," as long as that root of merit exists?
II. The exposition of the middle view is as before.
To some extent he has a desire for the welfare of others;
his meditation consists in the contemplation of a person (pudgala) who is free from permanence and impermanence by means of the concentration on inhalation and exhalation (ānāpāna-samādhi).
The state of motionlessness [induced] by the "water-pot" [meditation] is an impurity of concentration, because it brings about dullness.
III. The exposition establishing the selflessness (*nairātmyatā*) of the body for the superior disciple who accepts external objects.
Meditation consists in the vision of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala*) through the thorough knowledge of the four noble truths.
In this context, suffering (*duḥkha*) is to be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Conceptual construction is the origin and should be abandoned;
cessation is insight and should be realized;
the path is emptiness and should be cultivated.
The superimposition of the nature of Sadāśiva upon emptiness is the impurity of meditation (*dhyāna-mala*).
Furthermore, its specific distinction in vision (*dṛṣṭi*) is the performance of the welfare of others.
Regarding this, some say that the mild Śrāvaka, because his lineage (*gotra*) is fixed and because he lacks compassion, is indeed a Śākya-Buddha.
But others say: "All shall become Buddhas; there exists no one on earth who is incapable [of it].
Therefore, one should not despair in the pursuit of perfect enlightenment."
(6) Thus, even a mild śrāvaka among sentient beings will become a perfectly awakened one (samyaksambuddha);
however, it is considered that a certain fixed lineage depends upon a [particular] Buddha.
As for the middling [type], he is one who will become a pratyekabuddha.
But the superior [type] is one who becomes a Buddha after accomplishing [the path] over four incalculable eons.
(The Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas) I. The exposition of the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas is precisely that of the superior Śrāvaka.

And this is the cultivation of tranquility and insight consisting of the self-arisen wisdom of the non-teacher, characterized by the emptiness and inconceivability of the person who has entered the path.
In that regard, the cessation of the sense faculties is insight (*vipaśyanā*), the non-apprehension of a person is tranquility (*śamatha*), and the restraint of body, speech, and mind is tranquility.
This is his meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
In this context, meditation on the state of pleasure of the mind that is not yet asleep, and meditation on the state of deep sleep of the mind, constitute the impurity of samādhi.
Regarding these, in the former case, there is an entry into the doctrine of Bhāskara.
Thus it has been said: "When sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has vanished, one should diligently cultivate that state of the mind which then arises."
(7) Thus [it is said]. But in the other case, there is an entry into the Vaiśeṣika doctrine.
Regarding this, the venerable Nāgārjuna said: "For cognition that does not know is established by the analogy of sleep."
Just as knowledge that has ceased from the senses is considered specific cognition (vaiśeṣika) by the Vaiśeṣikas.

(8) The word of the Blessed One also says: "It would be better for me to become a jackal in the delightful Jeta Grove than to attain the liberation of the Vaiśeṣikas, which is like the state of a cow."
(9) Thus; the view is also as before.
This one also brings about the state of Buddhahood through four incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
II. Furthermore, the compassion (*karuṇā*) of these two—the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha—has sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambanā*).

That compassion which arises day after day by taking sentient beings as its object through the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) is "having sentient beings as its object.
The teaching of the Śrāvaka is verbal (*vācikī*), whereas that of the Pratyekabuddha is physical (*kāyikī*).
Thus it has been said: "In the absence of the appearance of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and upon the passing away of the Śrāvakas, the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas arises from non-association."
(10) (The Mahāyāna) (the system of the perfections).
I. Now, those practitioners of the system of the perfections are described.
Among them, the one of dull capacity is a Sautrāntika.
Indeed, this object, which consists of an accumulation of atoms, is the producer of cognition with an image (*sākārajñāna*).
And its very nature of being a producer of cognition with an image is precisely what constitutes its "examination" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*).
Regarding this, they say: "If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be the apprehended (*grāhya*), the wise understand its status as the apprehended [to be its causal efficacy]."
Those who know the reasoning [declare] that causality alone is capable of imparting its form to cognition.
(11) Thus is the commentary.
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the inconceivability of one whose collection of sense-faculties has turned away from sense-objects.
As it has been said: "This calculation of repetition consists of time and the number of actions."
Therefore, cultivation must be practiced.
And as for this cultivation: when one practices with the mind fixed through awakening, then I do not perceive the mind; where has it gone, and where could it abide?
(12) Even when one has become a householder, one should practice meditation... having assumed the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with the flickering mind fixed on the tip of the nose.
(13) The defilement of this samādhi is as before.

Through the non-apprehension of the triad, by means of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is the practice of the five perfections; the dedication of the fruit toward the welfare of sentient beings while being averse to [clinging to] that fruit—this is the view.
II. The middling practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*).

In this regard, the Proponent of Representational Consciousness (*sākāravijñānavādin*)—on the grounds that even atoms are untenable according to the reasoning beginning with, "Because of simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom would have six parts"—has established that this is nothing but mind-only (*cittamātra*), which assumes the forms of consciousness, is devoid of the state of grasped object and grasping subject, and shines as luminosity. As it has been said: "O Sons of the Victor, the triple world is indeed mind-only!"
And thus Kīrtipāda has said: "If cognition possesses a form such as blue and so forth, what is the basis for an external object?
If cognition does not possess a form such as blue and so forth, what is the basis for an external object?"
(14) Thus it is said.
It is also stated elsewhere:
(4) "The objects of the senses do not inherently exist as burdens within the mind."
For it is the mind alone that appears through the manifestation of form and so forth.

(15) Therefore, it is the explanation of the Yogācāra who maintains that consciousness possesses forms (*sākāravijñānavādin*): "It is mind alone, appearing in various forms, which manifests as something to be illuminated independently of anything else.
However, the Yogācāra who maintains that [consciousness] is formless (*nirākāravādin*) considers that this very mind is of the nature of self-cognition devoid of forms.
As it has been said: "An external object does not exist in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish."
The mind, stirred by latent impressions, proceeds as the appearance of objects.
Whatever appears and however it appears is indeed like an illusion;
for in reality, it is without appearance, resembling the pure and infinite sky.
(17) The Dharmakāya of the Great Sage is free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of appearance;
the two Form Bodies arise from it and subsequently abide like an illusion.
(18) Thus is the commentary.

For the proponent of the existence of mental images (*sākāravādin*), meditation (*dhyāna*) is the direct realization of the non-duality of the true mind, in which all conceptual constructions have been shaken off.
As it has been said: "Wherever the mind goes toward an object of knowledge, one should apply it right there."
Having moved, where will you go? For everything is indeed composed of that.

(19) Thus, for the proponent of formlessness (*nirākāravādin*), meditation (*dhyāna*) is the direct realization of a mind that is blissful, non-dual, inconceivable, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and without appearance (*nirābhāsa*).
And so it is said: "Its nature is considered to be transparent, formless, and stainless."
Indeed, it is never possible for one who is not a Buddha to know that.
(20) Even the thought "this is representation-only" is based on apprehension;
by placing something before oneself, one does not abide in that state of representation-only.
But when cognition no longer perceives an objective support,
then consciousness abides in the state of mere-consciousness (vijñaptimātra), because in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is no grasping.

(22) In the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on consciousness possessing forms which is ultimately real and eternal, there is the entry into the doctrine of the Lord who maintains the Vedānta position. For he maintains that the world— which is ultimately real, eternal, and of the nature of transformations non-different from Brahman whose essence is its own consciousness— is [identical with] Brahman.
And so it has been said: "Whatever indeed is seen, one should conceive that as Brahman;
then the mind, no longer directed toward anything else, abides in Brahman alone."
(23) Thus, this is the impurity of the Samāhita state for the proponents of *sākāra* (with-form).

Likewise, for the proponent of *nirākāra* (without-form) as well, there is the consequence of entering into the position of the Vedāntins who follow the doctrine of Bhāskara, through the cultivation of a self-cognizing consciousness (*svasaṃvedana-vijñāna*) that is eternal, free from appearances, and devoid of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
For he too accepts an eternal Brahman that is a mass of pure light and bliss, in which all the defilements of the conceptual proliferation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*) have been removed.
In me, who am the clear ocean of awakening, that reflection of the universal intellect—
whether it has arisen or dissolved— is not subject to conceptual construction.
(24) Thus ends the impurity of meditative absorption for the proponents of non-aspectarianism (*nirākāravādin*).
The view of these two is as explained previously.
III. The superior Mādhyamika.

In this regard, the commentary of those who propound non-duality as being like an illusion states: "The Madhyamikas know reality to be neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; it is entirely free from the four extremes."
And this is its meaning: it is not existent, because that which exists cannot be sublated; nor is it non-existent, because of the force of its manifestation.
Likewise, due to the fault of duality, neither both [existence and non-existence] nor neither both is possible, because there is likewise an absence of cognition.
Furthermore, from the consideration of the former and the latter: "Just as a form in a painting possesses the power of the object as it is, there is no attachment to the parts. (26)
For that is the explanation [of the phrase] "as non-dual like an illusion.
And the cultivation of this very non-duality like an illusion is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Any adherence to annihilation therein is merely a defilement of that meditative absorption.
Through the conviction that the two [truths] are like an illusion, there is the vision that fulfills the six perfections.
However, for those who teach the non-abiding of all phenomena, this is their analysis: The universe is not held to be eternal, nor is its annihilation intended;
Neither the pair of eternity and annihilation, nor anything other than both.

(27) The Buddhas know the reality of things as being entirely without foundation; furthermore, this conceptual construction does not exist at all, since consciousness does not perceive the state of being mind.
(28) Whatever is a superimposition of anything, all that is indeed not so in any way;
for the meaning of the Middle Way is free from superimposition—how, then, could there be negation or affirmation therein?
(29) For that gnosis which is effortless is declared to be inconceivable; indeed, if that which is inconceivable were to be conceived, it would not truly be inconceivable.
(30) For the wise one by whom the world is realized as unborn through pure awakening,
his own world is truly real, occurring without effort.
(31) Thus it has been said: "When the reality itself shines forth, naturally free from all superimpositions, the refutation of those superimpositions occurs through designations such as 'emptiness'."
(32) And the meditation (*dhyāna*) is the direct realization, through dwelling without attachment, of this very object that has arrived via investigation and which is free from superimposition.
The impurity of meditative absorption (*samādhi-mala*) is the state of insentience resulting from the annihilation of all objects.
The view (*dṛṣṭi*) is the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) without superimposition.
IV. Herein, for those of weak and middling faculties, compassion has phenomena as its object (*dharmālambanā*).
That which arises by taking as its object all phenomena that fall into the calamity of impermanence should be understood as having phenomena as its object.

For those of superior faculties, however, compassion has the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as its object; it is an objectless compassion (*anālambanā karuṇā*) because it is realized through mental attention to the fact that phenomena lack intrinsic nature.

The establishment of his three bodies has been taught by the protector Maitreya. And thus it is said: "That body of the Sage which, until the end of existence, unceasingly performs various benefits for the world equally, is the emanation body (nairmāṇika-kāya)."
(33) This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
is considered the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*), because it partakes in the enjoyment of the Mahāyāna.
(34) Those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in every aspect constitute the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of the Sage, characterized by their intrinsic nature.
(35) Thus.
(The Mantra Method:

However, the Mantra method (*mantranaya*) is not explained here by us because of its extreme profundity, because it is the domain of persons who have faith in the profound method, and because of the extensive nature of the explanations regarding the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) such as the four seals (*caturmudrā*).

And thus: (7) Even though the goal is the same, the science of mantras is superior because it brings freedom from confusion, possesses many methods, is not difficult to practice, and is intended for those with sharp faculties.
(36) Furthermore, we have composed here a treatise titled *Sekanirṇaya*.
[End. Now, if the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indeed that which is determined by the Mahāyāna, for what purpose did the Blessed One then teach the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles?
To this, it is replied: not so.

It is precisely for the sake of attaining that which is to be attained through the Mahāyāna that the two ladders of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles are fashioned. As it has been said: "In order to lead beginner beings into the ultimate truth, this skillful means was fashioned by the Perfectly Awakened Ones like a staircase."
It is also said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: "There is indeed but one vehicle, and but one method; this teaching of the Leaders is singular.
Such is my skill in means that I manifest three vehicles."
(38) It has also been stated by the venerable Nāgārjuna: "O Lord, because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is undifferentiated, there is no distinction among meditative absorptions;
yet the three vehicles were taught by you for the sake of introducing sentient beings [to the path]."
(39) It is also stated elsewhere: "Liberation, however, is the vision of emptiness; for its sake, there is the cultivation of all things.
(40) And this manifestation of the three vehicles should be understood by the Blessed One as being that very emptiness itself.
For thus it is: "O Lord, not even a single syllable was uttered by you;
yet the entire assembly of those to be trained has been satiated by the rain of the Dharma."
(41) Like a wish-fulfilling gem, he is unshakable by the winds of all conceptual constructions;
nevertheless, he fulfills the hopes of all sentient beings without exception.
(42) By means of the principle of the revolving wheel, even though the Protector is free from conceptual construction, the teaching proceeds through the power of his accumulated merit and wisdom.
(43) Indeed, there is no finality for the vehicles as long as the mind continues to function;
but when the mind has undergone revolution, there is neither vehicle nor traveler.
(44) For here the stainless speech, like a casket of the jewel of the True Dharma, has been strung together;
O wise ones, let this *Tattvaratnāvalī* be held in your hearts for the sake of joy.
(45) Since I am fond of conciseness and averse to prolixity, my extensive treatment of that unsurpassed subject must be forgiven by those who delight in detail.
(46) Having composed this treatise of unsurpassed meaning through my effort in seeking the welfare of those capable of liberation,
may the world, by whatever merit has been gained thereby, attain the state of a Tathāgata, which is otherwise unattainable.
(47) The *Tattvaratnāvalī* is completed. This work is by the venerable scholar-adept Advayavajra. (9)
